claim: Neuromesodermal progenitors are a single Sox2lowTlow entity whose choice of neural or mesodermal fate is dictated by their position in the progenitor region.
source: Here we show that neuromesodermal progenitors are a single Sox2lowTlow entity whose choice of neural or mesodermal fate is dictated by their position in the progenitor region.
evidence: Supported by grafting experiments showing equivalent potential of rostral CLE cells when transplanted to NSB, and by quantitative analysis of Sox2 and T expression levels in different progenitor regions.

claim: The choice of mesoderm fate in neuromesodermal progenitors is Wnt/β-catenin dependent.
source: The choice of mesoderm fate is Wnt/β-catenin dependent.
evidence: Demonstrated by grafting experiments where β-catenin deletion in L1-3 cells caused a switch from mesoderm to neural fate.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signalling is required for a previously unrecognised phase of progenitor expansion during mid-trunk formation.
source: Wnt/β-catenin signalling is also required for a previously unrecognised phase of progenitor expansion during mid-trunk formation.
evidence: Supported by quantification showing Sox2+T+ cell numbers peak at E9.5 and fail to expand in β-catenin-deleted embryos.

claim: Lateral/ventral mesoderm progenitors represent a distinct committed state that is unable to differentiate to neural fates.
source: Lateral/ventral mesoderm progenitors represent a distinct committed state that is unable to differentiate to neural fates, even upon overexpression of the neural transcription factor Sox2.
evidence: Demonstrated by grafting L/St5 cells to neural-promoting locations and by Sox2 overexpression experiments, both showing failure to adopt neural fate.

claim: Lateral/ventral mesoderm progenitors do not require Wnt/β-catenin signalling for mesoderm differentiation.
source: They do not require Wnt/β-catenin signalling for mesoderm differentiation.
evidence: Shown by grafting β-catenin-deleted L/St5 cells which still formed mesoderm without neural differentiation.

claim: The rostrocaudal axis is supplied by populations of progenitors at the caudal end of the embryo.
source: The rostrocaudal (head-to-tail) axis is supplied by populations of progenitors at the caudal end of the embryo.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field of developmental biology.

claim: Clonal analysis has demonstrated the presence of axial progenitors that behave as dual-fated tissue stem cells of the neurectoderm and somitic mesoderm.
source: Clonal analysis has demonstrated the presence of axial progenitors that behave as dual-fated tissue stem cells of the neurectoderm and somitic mesoderm (Tzouanacou et al., 2009), termed neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous clonal analysis study.

claim: The dorsal layer of the bilayered Node-Streak Border (NSB) and the Caudal Lateral Epiblast (CLE) are regions of dual neurectoderm and mesoderm fate at early somite stages.
source: Population fate maps at early somite stages have identified two regions of dual neurectoderm and mesoderm fate: the dorsal layer of the bilayered Node-Streak Border (NSB) and the Caudal Lateral Epiblast (CLE) on either side of the PS.
evidence: Based on previous fate mapping studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The NSB gives rise to the majority of the neuromesoderm-fated chordoneural hinge (CNH) in the tail bud.
source: The NSB also gives rise to the majority of the neuromesoderm-fated chordoneural hinge (CNH) in the tail bud (Cambray and Wilson, 2002; 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous fate mapping studies.

claim: The adjacent midline PS and rostral node (RN) are fated exclusively for mesoderm and notochord, respectively.
source: The adjacent midline PS and rostral node (RN) are fated exclusively for mesoderm and notochord, respectively (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by fate mapping data and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The caudal-most tip of the CLE and the adjoining caudal primitive streak are solely fated for lateral/ventral mesoderm (LVM).
source: The caudal-most tip of the CLE, and the adjoining caudal primitive streak, are solely fated for lateral/ventral mesoderm (LVM) (Cambray and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: Based on previous fate mapping studies.

claim: Cell fate in and around the primitive streak is highly regionalised.
source: Thus cell fate in and around the PS is highly regionalised.
evidence: Inferred from the described regional differences in fate mapping results.

claim: Fate mapping studies indicate a rostrocaudal organisation of mesoderm progenitors within the primitive streak.
source: Fate mapping studies in early somite-stage mouse and chick embryos indicate a rostrocaudal organisation of mesoderm progenitors within the PS.
evidence: Supported by multiple cited fate mapping studies in mouse and chick.

claim: Midline mesoderm is produced by the rostral primitive streak.
source: Midline mesoderm is produced by the rostral PS, while successively more caudal regions of the streak are fated for the paraxial and lateral mesoderm (Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Brown and Storey, 2000; Catala et al., 1996; Schoenwolf, 1992; Wilson and Beddington, 1996).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited fate mapping studies.

claim: Successively more caudal regions of the primitive streak are fated for the paraxial and lateral mesoderm.
source: Midline mesoderm is produced by the rostral PS, while successively more caudal regions of the streak are fated for the paraxial and lateral mesoderm (Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Brown and Storey, 2000; Catala et al., 1996; Schoenwolf, 1992; Wilson and Beddington, 1996).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited fate mapping studies.

claim: Cells fated exclusively for the medial somite in the NSB can be re-fated to more lateral regions of the somite on transplantation to the anterior primitive streak.
source: We have previously shown that cells fated exclusively for the medial somite in the NSB can be re-fated to more lateral regions of the somite on transplantation to the anterior primitive streak (Cambray and Wilson, 2007), indicating a degree of plasticity in paraxial mesoderm (PXM) fates.
evidence: Based on previous transplantation experiments by the authors.

claim: Paraxial mesoderm fates exhibit a degree of plasticity.
source: We have previously shown that cells fated exclusively for the medial somite in the NSB can be re-fated to more lateral regions of the somite on transplantation to the anterior primitive streak (Cambray and Wilson, 2007), indicating a degree of plasticity in paraxial mesoderm (PXM) fates.
evidence: Inferred from the re-fating experiment results.

claim: Fate maps of the CLE in chick indicate that cells at the rostral or lateral edges form more neurectoderm than those at caudal or medial positions.
source: Fate maps of the CLE in chick indicate that cells at the rostral or lateral edges of the CLE form more neurectoderm than those at caudal or medial positions, which tend to generate mesoderm (Brown and Storey, 2000; Iimura et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited fate mapping studies in chick.

claim: Cells at caudal or medial positions of the CLE tend to generate mesoderm.
source: Fate maps of the CLE in chick indicate that cells at the rostral or lateral edges of the CLE form more neurectoderm than those at caudal or medial positions, which tend to generate mesoderm (Brown and Storey, 2000; Iimura et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited fate mapping studies in chick.

claim: CLE progenitors are more transitory than those in the NSB.
source: Furthermore, fate maps of mouse and chick have suggested that CLE progenitors are more transitory than those in the NSB, since they do not contribute to long axial stretches or extensively to the CNH (Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Brown and Storey, 2000; Iimura et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on fate mapping studies showing limited contribution of CLE cells.

claim: CLE progenitors do not contribute to long axial stretches or extensively to the CNH.
source: Furthermore, fate maps of mouse and chick have suggested that CLE progenitors are more transitory than those in the NSB, since they do not contribute to long axial stretches or extensively to the CNH (Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Brown and Storey, 2000; Iimura et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited fate mapping studies.

claim: T, Tbx6, Fgfr1 and Wnt3a are expressed in the primitive streak region and required for correct mesoderm production.
source: T, Tbx6, Fgfr1 and Wnt3a are expressed in the PS region and required for correct mesoderm production, and loss of each of them leads both to shortened axes, and the ectopic production of neural tissue at the expense of somitic mesoderm (Chapman and Papaioannou, 1998; Yamaguchi et al., 1999; Yoshikawa et al., 1997; Ciruna et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited genetic studies.

claim: Loss of T, Tbx6, Fgfr1 or Wnt3a leads to shortened axes and ectopic production of neural tissue at the expense of somitic mesoderm.
source: T, Tbx6, Fgfr1 and Wnt3a are expressed in the PS region and required for correct mesoderm production, and loss of each of them leads both to shortened axes, and the ectopic production of neural tissue at the expense of somitic mesoderm (Chapman and Papaioannou, 1998; Yamaguchi et al., 1999; Yoshikawa et al., 1997; Ciruna et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited genetic studies.

claim: NMP maintenance is intimately linked with preserving a balance between neurectoderm and mesoderm production.
source: This suggests that NMP maintenance is intimately linked with preserving a balance between neurectoderm and mesoderm production.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of key genes leads to neural tissue production at the expense of mesoderm.

claim: Tbx6 expression in the midline primitive streak represses Sox2 in mesoderm-fated cells, ensuring suppression of the neural transcription program.
source: Tbx6 expression in the midline PS represses Sox2 in mesoderm-fated cells, ensuring suppression of the neural transcription program (Takemoto et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited molecular study.

claim: In zebrafish, Wnt/β-catenin activation influences the decision of cells in both gastrula- and somite-stage embryos to enter neural or mesodermal lineages.
source: Furthermore, in zebrafish, Wnt/β-catenin activation influences the decision of cells in both gastrula- and somite-stage embryos to enter neural or mesodermal lineages (Martin and Kimelman, 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited study in zebrafish.

claim: Conditional deletion of Wnt3a or β-catenin in the T+ cell compartment leads to a switch of primitive streak progenitors towards a neural fate.
source: More recently, lineage-tracing experiments showed that conditional deletion of Wnt3a or β-catenin in the T+ cell compartment leads to a switch of primitive streak progenitors towards a neural fate (Garriock et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited lineage-tracing study.

claim: Constitutive Wnt/β-catenin activity in the T+ cell compartment is not sufficient to divert all neural progenitors to mesoderm fates.
source: However, constitutive Wnt/β-catenin activity in the T+ cell compartment is not sufficient to divert all neural progenitors to mesoderm fates: providing cells in the caudal progenitor region with a stabilised form of β-catenin results in an enlarged PSM domain, but does not lead to loss of neural cell production (Aulehla et al., 2008; Jurberg et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited genetic manipulation studies.

claim: Providing cells in the caudal progenitor region with a stabilised form of β-catenin results in an enlarged PSM domain but does not lead to loss of neural cell production.
source: However, constitutive Wnt/β-catenin activity in the T+ cell compartment is not sufficient to divert all neural progenitors to mesoderm fates: providing cells in the caudal progenitor region with a stabilised form of β-catenin results in an enlarged PSM domain, but does not lead to loss of neural cell production (Aulehla et al., 2008; Jurberg et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited genetic manipulation studies.

claim: Enhanced β-catenin activity does not necessarily compromise the presence of NMPs in the CLE.
source: Moreover, enhanced β-catenin activity does not necessarily compromise the presence of NMPs in the CLE (Garriock et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited study.

claim: NMPs are committed to neuromesodermal lineages.
source: We find that NMPs are committed to neuromesodermal lineages and choose between retention as progenitors, and differentiation as either neurectoderm or mesoderm based on their location within the progenitor region; the latter choice is β-catenin dependent.
evidence: Demonstrated by kidney capsule grafts showing restriction to neural and mesodermal derivatives.

claim: NMPs choose between retention as progenitors and differentiation as either neurectoderm or mesoderm based on their location within the progenitor region.
source: We find that NMPs are committed to neuromesodermal lineages and choose between retention as progenitors, and differentiation as either neurectoderm or mesoderm based on their location within the progenitor region; the latter choice is β-catenin dependent.
evidence: Demonstrated by heterotopic grafting experiments showing position-dependent fate outcomes.

claim: NMPs express low levels of T and Sox2.
source: We show that NMPs express low levels of T and Sox2, and that during mid-trunk formation, Wnt/β-catenin signalling expands the number of Sox2+T+ NMPs and maintains the appropriate level of T in the NMP population.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative 3D analysis of Sox2 and T protein levels showing NMPs are excluded from high-expressing regions.

claim: During mid-trunk formation, Wnt/β-catenin signalling expands the number of Sox2+T+ NMPs.
source: We show that NMPs express low levels of T and Sox2, and that during mid-trunk formation, Wnt/β-catenin signalling expands the number of Sox2+T+ NMPs and maintains the appropriate level of T in the NMP population.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification showing failure of Sox2+T+ cell expansion in β-catenin-deleted embryos.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signalling maintains the appropriate level of T in the NMP population during mid-trunk formation.
source: We show that NMPs express low levels of T and Sox2, and that during mid-trunk formation, Wnt/β-catenin signalling expands the number of Sox2+T+ NMPs and maintains the appropriate level of T in the NMP population.
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D analysis showing dramatic downregulation of T in NMPs when β-catenin is depleted.

claim: Lateral/ventral mesoderm progenitors show plasticity within the mesoderm lineage.
source: We further show that lateral/ventral mesoderm progenitors are exclusively mesoderm-committed yet show plasticity within the mesoderm lineage, and respond to distinct signalling and transcription factor cues from those that govern NMPs.
evidence: Demonstrated by grafting L/St5 cells to rostral PS, showing contribution to both PXM and LVM.

claim: Lateral/ventral mesoderm progenitors respond to distinct signalling and transcription factor cues from those that govern NMPs.
source: We further show that lateral/ventral mesoderm progenitors are exclusively mesoderm-committed yet show plasticity within the mesoderm lineage, and respond to distinct signalling and transcription factor cues from those that govern NMPs.
evidence: Demonstrated by β-catenin deletion and Sox2 overexpression experiments showing different responses compared to NMPs.

claim: Control grafts of E7.5 anterior or posterior parts of the late-streak or early headfold stage embryo formed large teratocarcinomas containing embryonal carcinoma cells and derivatives of all three germ layers.
source: Control grafts of embryonic day (E) 7.5 anterior (rostral) or posterior (caudal, PS-containing) parts of the late-streak or early headfold stage embryo formed large teratocarcinomas containing embryonal carcinoma (EC) cells and derivatives of all three germ layers including neural and non-neural ectoderm (Beddington, 1983; Osorno et al., 2012).
evidence: Demonstrated by kidney capsule grafting experiments and histological analysis.

claim: E8.5 (2–6 somite) grafts gave rise to smaller tissue masses containing only well-differentiated tissues and no embryonal carcinoma cells.
source: In contrast, E8.5 (2–6 somite) grafts gave rise to smaller tissue masses containing only well-differentiated tissues and no EC cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by kidney capsule grafting experiments and histological analysis.

claim: NSB, CLE (L1-3) and most CNH grafts gave rise only to neural and mesodermal derivatives.
source: NSB, CLE (L1-3) and most (4/5) CNH grafts gave rise only to neural and mesodermal derivatives, although one CNH graft included keratinised epithelium, possibly through contamination from neighbouring specified surface ectoderm cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by kidney capsule grafting experiments and histological analysis.

claim: Grafts of the caudal CLE and neighbouring midline (L/St5) produced very small growths devoid of neurectoderm.
source: Grafts of the caudal CLE and neighbouring midline (L/St5), both of which produce LVM (Cambray and Wilson, 2007), produced very small growths devoid of neurectoderm.
evidence: Demonstrated by kidney capsule grafting experiments and histological analysis.

claim: Rostral PS (St1) grafts predominantly produced adipocytes.
source: Rostral PS (St1) grafts predominantly produced adipocytes, while rostral node (RN) grafts produced mainly neurectoderm.
evidence: Demonstrated by kidney capsule grafting experiments and histological analysis.

claim: Rostral node (RN) grafts produced mainly neurectoderm.
source: Rostral PS (St1) grafts predominantly produced adipocytes, while rostral node (RN) grafts produced mainly neurectoderm.
evidence: Demonstrated by kidney capsule grafting experiments and histological analysis.

claim: NM-fated cells in ≥E8.5 embryonic regions are not pluripotent but restricted in potency to neural and mesoderm fates.
source: Therefore, NM-fated cells in ≥E8.5 embryonic regions are not pluripotent but restricted in potency to neural and mesoderm fates, while LVM-fated cells produce only mesoderm.
evidence: Inferred from kidney capsule grafting results showing lineage restriction.

claim: LVM-fated cells produce only mesoderm.
source: Therefore, NM-fated cells in ≥E8.5 embryonic regions are not pluripotent but restricted in potency to neural and mesoderm fates, while LVM-fated cells produce only mesoderm.
evidence: Demonstrated by kidney capsule grafting experiments showing mesoderm-only derivatives.

claim: Coexpression of Sox2 and T colocalises with regions of NM fate in the mouse E8.5 caudal region.
source: We recently showed that coexpression of Sox2 and T colocalises with regions of NM fate in the mouse E8.5 caudal region (Tsakiridis et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on previous study by the authors.

claim: Sox2 and T coexpression has been reported to identify similar regions in zebrafish, chick and human.
source: This combinatorial marker has also been reported to identify similar regions in zebrafish, chick and human (Martin and Kimelman, 2012; Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited studies in other species.

claim: Sox2+T+ cells were first detected in the epiblast close to the NSB of the E7.5 (late bud stage) embryo.
source: Wholemount in situ hybridisation and immunofluorescence showed that Sox2+T+ cells were first detected in the epiblast close to the NSB of the E7.5 (late bud stage) embryo (Figure 3Ba,b).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridisation and immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: At E8.5, Sox2 expression was strong in the differentiating neurectoderm and weaker in the CLE.
source: At E8.5 the expression of Sox2 transcripts and protein was strong in the differentiating neurectoderm, and weaker in the CLE, while T expression in the CLE was most prominent caudally in the PS (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridisation and immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: At E8.5, T expression in the CLE was most prominent caudally in the primitive streak.
source: At E8.5 the expression of Sox2 transcripts and protein was strong in the differentiating neurectoderm, and weaker in the CLE, while T expression in the CLE was most prominent caudally in the PS (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridisation and immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: During trunk and tail formation, Sox2/T coexpression persisted in the CNH and surrounding areas (E9.5–13.5).
source: During trunk and tail formation, Sox2/T coexpression persisted in the CNH and surrounding areas (E9.5–13.5; Figure 3B–D and 9Ca–c).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figures 3 and 9.

claim: At E13.5, just before elongation had ceased, a few Sox2+T+ cells could still be detected.
source: At E13.5, just before elongation had ceased, a few Sox2+T+ cells could still be detected, whereas once axial elongation was complete, Sox2+T+ cells had disappeared.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: Once axial elongation was complete, Sox2+T+ cells had disappeared.
source: At E13.5, just before elongation had ceased, a few Sox2+T+ cells could still be detected, whereas once axial elongation was complete, Sox2+T+ cells had disappeared.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: At E14.5, T expression was detected in the caudal notochord, while Sox2 expression was absent.
source: At E14.5, T expression was detected in the caudal notochord, while Sox2 expression was absent, consistent with the absence of the NT by this stage (Figure 3D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridisation and immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Sox2+T+ cells are found at all known locations and times that NMPs are present.
source: Thus, Sox2+T+ cells are found at all known locations and times that NMPs are present.
evidence: Inferred from the spatiotemporal correlation between Sox2+T+ cells and known NMP locations.

claim: The majority of Sox2+T+ cells described a 'U' shape in the epiblast at E8.5 including the NSB and L1-3, coinciding with NMP locations.
source: The majority of Sox2+T+ cells described a 'U' shape in the epiblast at E8.5 including the NSB and L1-3, coinciding with NMP locations (Figure 4Aa,b).
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The total number of cells labelled with Sox2 or T increased up to E10.5, decreasing thereafter.
source: The total number of cells labelled with either marker increased up to E10.5, decreasing thereafter, while Sox2+T+ cell numbers showed a similar profile but peaked at E9.5.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data.

claim: Sox2+T+ cell numbers showed a similar profile to total labelled cells but peaked at E9.5.
source: The total number of cells labelled with either marker increased up to E10.5, decreasing thereafter, while Sox2+T+ cell numbers showed a similar profile but peaked at E9.5.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data.

claim: Sox2+T+ cells were rare at E13.5, and undetectable by E14.5.
source: Sox2+T+ cells were rare at E13.5, and undetectable by E14.5 (Figure 4B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E and Video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data shown in figures.

claim: The number of putative NMPs peaks during mid-trunk formation.
source: Thus the number of putative NMPs peaks during mid-trunk formation.
evidence: Inferred from the quantification showing peak Sox2+T+ cell numbers at E9.5.

claim: At E8.5, the levels of T were lower in the lateral than the medial CLE and the primitive streak.
source: At E8.5 the levels of T were lower in the lateral than the medial CLE and the PS.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative 3D analysis of T protein levels.

claim: T expression was high and ubiquitous in L/St5.
source: T expression was high and ubiquitous in L/St5.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative 3D analysis of T protein levels.

claim: The highest levels of T were found in the notochord.
source: The highest levels of T were found in the notochord.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative 3D analysis of T protein levels.

claim: Sox2 was detected in a rostral-to-caudal gradient, with higher expression levels found rostrally.
source: Sox2 was detected in a rostral-to-caudal gradient, with higher expression levels found rostrally (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative 3D analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sox2+T+ cells were excluded from high Sox2 and high T expressing regions.
source: Strikingly, Sox2+T+ cells were excluded from high Sox2 and high T expressing regions (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative 3D analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The levels of Sox2 and T in individual cells may reflect greater likelihood to adopt neural and mesodermal fates respectively.
source: Strikingly, Sox2+T+ cells were excluded from high Sox2 and high T expressing regions (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between expression levels and fate outcomes in grafting experiments.

claim: Small numbers of Sox2+T+ cells were observed in the midline primitive streak at E8.5.
source: We observed small numbers of Sox2+T+ cells in regions not expected to harbour NMPs, such as the midline PS at E8.5, suggesting that although NM progenitor identity and Sox2/T positivity substantially overlap, either this correspondence is not absolute, or previous grafting studies (Cambray and Wilson, 2007) may not detect low proportions of NMPs.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative 3D analysis of Sox2 and T expression.

claim: Some ingressed primitive streak cells behave similarly to cells in the epiblast when Wnt3a is lost.
source: Using a Cited1-CreERT2-labelling system (tracing mesodermal and hindgut lineages), Garriock et al. found that some ingressed PS cells behave similarly to cells in the epiblast when Wnt3a is lost (Garriock et al., 2015), implying that some Sox2+T+ cells in the PS might retain NMP potential during early mesoderm differentiation.
evidence: Based on cited lineage-tracing study.

claim: At E8.5, the numbers of Sox2+T+ cells were highest in L1, declining towards L3.
source: Interestingly, at E8.5, the numbers of Sox2+T+ cells were highest in L1, declining towards L3.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data.

claim: The medial CLE contained more Sox2+T+ cells than lateral CLE.
source: Furthermore, the medial CLE contained more Sox2+T+ cells than lateral CLE ( Figure 3Bc–f and 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The graded rostral-to-caudal decline in Sox2 and increase in T suggest cellular heterogeneity within the CLE.
source: Together with the graded rostral-to-caudal decline in Sox2 and increase in T, these results suggest cellular heterogeneity within the CLE.
evidence: Inferred from the observed gradients in Sox2 and T expression.

claim: Five of 11 L1 grafts (L1A grafts) gave rise to differentiated regions of the axis and did not contribute to the tail bud.
source: Five of 11 L1 grafts (L1-axis, 'L1A' grafts) gave rise to differentiated regions of the axis and did not contribute to the TB.
evidence: Demonstrated by homotopic grafting experiments and sectional analysis.

claim: L1A grafts contributed extensively and unilaterally to neurectoderm.
source: These contributed extensively and unilaterally to neurectoderm (Figure 6Aa–d), and at lower frequency to mesoderm, predominantly (in 31/36 sections) unilaterally (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by homotopic grafting experiments and sectional analysis shown in figures.

claim: L1A grafts contributed to mesoderm at lower frequency than neurectoderm, predominantly unilaterally.
source: These contributed extensively and unilaterally to neurectoderm (Figure 6Aa–d), and at lower frequency to mesoderm, predominantly (in 31/36 sections) unilaterally (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by homotopic grafting experiments and sectional analysis shown in figures.

claim: The failure of L1A grafts to contribute to the tail bud shows that these cells are en route for exit from the progenitor region.
source: The failure of L1A grafts to contribute to the TB shows that these cells are en route for exit from the progenitor region, and the unilateral mesoderm contribution suggests that this mesoderm was already formed and carried alongside the CLE graft rather than ingressing through the PS.
evidence: Inferred from the grafting results and contribution patterns.

claim: The unilateral mesoderm contribution in L1A grafts suggests that this mesoderm was already formed and carried alongside the CLE graft rather than ingressing through the primitive streak.
source: The failure of L1A grafts to contribute to the TB shows that these cells are en route for exit from the progenitor region, and the unilateral mesoderm contribution suggests that this mesoderm was already formed and carried alongside the CLE graft rather than ingressing through the PS.
evidence: Inferred from the unilateral contribution pattern and comparison with bilateral contributions in other grafts.

claim: The presomitic mesoderm underlying the CLE contributes only to short stretches of axial tissue (estimated ~6 somites).
source: This is in agreement with previous reports that the presomitic mesoderm underlying the CLE contributes only to short stretches of axial tissue (estimated ~6 somites) (Nicolas et al., 1996; Tam, 1986; 1988) (see also Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by cited previous studies and source data.

claim: The remaining six L1 grafts (L1AT), as well as 9/10 L2-3 homotopic grafts, contributed from a variable rostral limit as far as the tail bud.
source: The remaining six L1 grafts (L1-axis/tail, 'L1AT'), as well as 9/10 L2-3 homotopic grafts, contributed from a variable rostral limit as far as the tail bud (Figure 6Ae–l).
evidence: Demonstrated by homotopic grafting experiments and sectional analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: L1AT and L2-3 grafts all contributed extensively and bilaterally to mesoderm.
source: These grafts all contributed extensively and bilaterally to mesoderm, the latter indicating that the mesodermal component had passed through the PS (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by homotopic grafting experiments and sectional analysis shown in figure supplement.

claim: Bilateral mesoderm contribution indicates that the mesodermal component had passed through the primitive streak.
source: These grafts all contributed extensively and bilaterally to mesoderm, the latter indicating that the mesodermal component had passed through the PS (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Inferred from the bilateral distribution pattern and known cell movements.

claim: Nearly all (15/16) L1AT and L2-3 grafts contributed to the tail bud mesoderm.
source: Nearly all (15/16) L1AT and L2-3 grafts contributed to the TBM, but only L1AT grafts consistently colonised the CNH, indicating that L1 contains putative NMPs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by homotopic grafting experiments and sectional analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Only L1AT grafts consistently colonised the chordoneural hinge, indicating that L1 contains putative NMPs.
source: Nearly all (15/16) L1AT and L2-3 grafts contributed to the TBM, but only L1AT grafts consistently colonised the CNH, indicating that L1 contains putative NMPs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by homotopic grafting experiments and inferred from CNH contribution pattern.

claim: Only L1 grafts showed significant neural contribution in the axis.
source: Strikingly, only L1 grafts showed significant neural contribution in the axis, while both L1 and L2-3 grafts contributed to mesoderm.
evidence: Demonstrated by homotopic grafting experiments and sectional analysis.

claim: Both L1 and L2-3 grafts contributed to mesoderm.
source: Strikingly, only L1 grafts showed significant neural contribution in the axis, while both L1 and L2-3 grafts contributed to mesoderm.
evidence: Demonstrated by homotopic grafting experiments and sectional analysis.

claim: Most neural-fated progenitors are in the rostral-most CLE.
source: Thus, most neural-fated progenitors are in the rostral-most CLE and the boundary between short-term (LB and L1A) and long-term (L1AT) progenitors lies within the L1 region.
evidence: Inferred from the differential neural contribution patterns of L1 versus L2-3 grafts.

claim: The boundary between short-term and long-term progenitors lies within the L1 region.
source: Thus, most neural-fated progenitors are in the rostral-most CLE and the boundary between short-term (LB and L1A) and long-term (L1AT) progenitors lies within the L1 region.
evidence: Inferred from the differential tail bud contribution patterns of L1A versus L1AT grafts.

claim: When donor cells were grafted in a more lateral position (L2lat), their descendants colonised mainly the lateral and dorsal neural tube.
source: However, when donor cells were grafted in a more lateral position (L2lat), their descendants colonised mainly the lateral and dorsal neural tube.
evidence: Demonstrated by mediolateral grafting experiments and sectional analysis.

claim: L2lat grafts showed low mesoderm contribution, largely unilateral and found at the rostral limit of the labelled part of the axis.
source: In contrast, contribution to the mesoderm was low, largely unilateral and found at the rostral limit of the labelled part of the axis (in 10/12 sections; Figure 6—figure supplement 4B), suggesting this contribution might have originated largely from co-grafted committed presomitic mesoderm cells at the start of culture.
evidence: Demonstrated by mediolateral grafting experiments and sectional analysis shown in figure supplement.

claim: The mesoderm contribution in L2lat grafts might have originated largely from co-grafted committed presomitic mesoderm cells.
source: In contrast, contribution to the mesoderm was low, largely unilateral and found at the rostral limit of the labelled part of the axis (in 10/12 sections; Figure 6—figure supplement 4B), suggesting this contribution might have originated largely from co-grafted committed presomitic mesoderm cells at the start of culture.
evidence: Inferred from the unilateral and rostral-limited distribution pattern.

claim: While NM fate is found in both medial and lateral CLE, cells in lateral positions are more likely to adopt neural (particularly dorsolateral) fates.
source: Thus, while NM fate is found in both medial and lateral CLE, cells in lateral positions are more likely to adopt neural (particularly dorsolateral) fates.
evidence: Inferred from the mediolateral grafting experiment results.

claim: All homotopic L/St5 grafts displayed consistent LVM contribution to a small stretch of the post-hindlimb axis.
source: All homotopic L/St5 grafts displayed consistent LVM contribution to a small stretch of the post-hindlimb axis.
evidence: Demonstrated by homotopic grafting experiments and sectional analysis.

claim: Homotopic L2-3 grafts displayed low but reproducible LVM contribution distributed throughout the labelled stretch of axis (20% of sections in 80% of embryos).
source: While homotopic L2-3 grafts displayed low but reproducible LVM contribution distributed throughout the labelled stretch of axis (20% of sections in 80% of embryos; Figure 6Aj and Figure 10—figure supplement 1A), LVM contribution was very rare in L1 grafts (<1% of sections in 9% of embryos; Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of homotopic grafting experiments shown in figure supplement.

claim: LVM contribution was very rare in L1 grafts (<1% of sections in 9% of embryos).
source: While homotopic L2-3 grafts displayed low but reproducible LVM contribution distributed throughout the labelled stretch of axis (20% of sections in 80% of embryos; Figure 6Aj and Figure 10—figure supplement 1A), LVM contribution was very rare in L1 grafts (<1% of sections in 9% of embryos; Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of homotopic grafting experiments shown in figure supplement.

claim: L/St5 is the only region to contribute exclusively to LVM.
source: Thus, L/St5 is the only region to contribute exclusively to LVM (Figure 6Au–w, Figure 10—figure supplement 1A and Cambray and Wilson (2007)).
evidence: Demonstrated by homotopic grafting experiments and comparison with other regions.

claim: Neural and mesodermal fate is more highly regionalised than previously appreciated in the rostral CLE (L1-3).
source: These homotopic grafts show that neural and mesodermal fate is more highly regionalised than previously appreciated.
evidence: Inferred from the detailed fate mapping results showing position-dependent outcomes.

claim: Cells in the caudal and medial parts of the CLE are more likely to adopt paraxial mesodermal fates.
source: In the rostral CLE (L1-3), cells in the caudal and medial parts of the CLE are more likely to adopt paraxial mesodermal fates, while the rostral and lateral CLE favours neural fates.
evidence: Inferred from the homotopic grafting results showing regional fate biases.

claim: The rostral and lateral CLE favours neural fates.
source: In the rostral CLE (L1-3), cells in the caudal and medial parts of the CLE are more likely to adopt paraxial mesodermal fates, while the rostral and lateral CLE favours neural fates.
evidence: Inferred from the homotopic grafting results showing regional fate biases.

claim: Regional fates correlate with the relative levels of Sox2 and T, with higher levels predicting neural/neuromesodermal and mesodermal fates respectively.
source: These fates correlate with the relative levels of Sox2 and T, higher levels of which appear to predict neural/ neuromesodermal and mesodermal fates respectively.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between expression levels and fate outcomes.

claim: The caudal CLE (L/St5), which expresses no Sox2, adopts exclusively lateral/ventral mesoderm fates.
source: The caudal CLE (L/St5), which expresses no Sox2, adopts exclusively lateral/ventral mesoderm fates.
evidence: Demonstrated by expression analysis and homotopic grafting experiments.

claim: The relative contribution to neural or mesodermal fates in the axis varied extensively between grafts of rostral CLE (L1-3) to NSB.
source: Strikingly, the relative contribution to neural or mesodermal fates in the axis varied extensively between grafts of rostral CLE (L1-3) to NSB (embryos 4.01–4.09; Figure 7A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated by heterotopic grafting experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Both L1-to-NSB and L2-3-to-NSB grafts appeared indistinguishable, with about half of the embryos in each class containing neural contribution of differing extents.
source: However, both L1-to-NSB and L2-3-to-NSB grafts appeared indistinguishable, with about half of the embryos in each class containing neural contribution of differing extents.
evidence: Demonstrated by heterotopic grafting experiments separating L1 from L2-3.

claim: Medial or lateral L1 or L2 grafts to NSB did not show consistent differences in neural or mesodermal differentiation.
source: However, these grafts did not show consistent differences in neural or mesodermal differentiation, and some grafts reversed their predicted fate (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by mediolateral heterotopic grafting experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Neither the neural fate of L1 and Llat, nor the mesodermal fate of L2-3 were retained after heterotopic grafting to the NSB.
source: Thus neither the neural fate of L1 and Llat, nor the mesodermal fate of L2-3 were retained after heterotopic grafting to the NSB, and therefore could not account for the variable neural and mesodermal contribution seen in individual grafted embryos.
evidence: Demonstrated by heterotopic grafting experiments showing fate changes.

claim: The fate differences seen in different CLE areas cannot be explained by ≥2 localised populations of restricted potential.
source: Consequently, the fate differences seen in different CLE areas cannot be explained by ≥2 localised populations of restricted potential.
evidence: Inferred from the failure to find consistent intrinsic fate biases in heterotopic grafts.

claim: Rostral CLE cells placed in either Br or Bm tended to contribute entirely, or predominantly, to neural tube.
source: Rostral CLE cells placed in either Br or Bm tended to contribute entirely, or predominantly, to neural tube, while grafts to Bc resulted in a high proportion of embryos with mesoderm-only contribution.
evidence: Demonstrated by position-specific heterotopic grafting experiments within the NSB.

claim: Grafts to Bc resulted in a high proportion of embryos with mesoderm-only contribution.
source: Rostral CLE cells placed in either Br or Bm tended to contribute entirely, or predominantly, to neural tube, while grafts to Bc resulted in a high proportion of embryos with mesoderm-only contribution.
evidence: Demonstrated by position-specific heterotopic grafting experiments within the NSB.

claim: The position within the NSB reversed the predicted fate bias of L1 towards neural and L2-3 towards mesodermal fates in several embryos.
source: In several embryos, the position within the NSB reversed the predicted fate bias of L1 towards neural and L2-3 towards mesodermal fates: 5/5 L2-3-to-Br grafts contributed to the NT, while embryo 6.21, an L1 graft, gave rise exclusively to mesoderm (Figure 7F).
evidence: Demonstrated by position-specific heterotopic grafting experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Assignment of rostral CLE cells to neural or mesodermal fates is dependent on environmental cues, with no detectable cell-intrinsic biases.
source: Thus our data indicate that assignment of rostral CLE cells to neural or mesodermal fates is dependent on environmental cues, with no detectable cell-intrinsic biases.
evidence: Inferred from the position-dependent fate outcomes in heterotopic grafting experiments.

claim: The data indicate a single NMP type capable of context-specific neural or mesodermal differentiation and retention in the progenitor region.
source: This data therefore indicates a single NMP type capable of context-specific neural or mesodermal differentiation and retention in the progenitor region.
evidence: Inferred from the equivalent potential of different CLE regions when placed in the same environment.

claim: CLE-derived cells were detected in the caudal notochord but did not express the notochord marker Foxa2 or high levels of T.
source: CLE-derived cells were detected in the caudal notochord (Figure 6—figure supplement 3). However, these cells did not express the notochord marker Foxa2, nor the high levels of T expressed in neighbouring host notochord cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry on grafted embryos shown in figure supplement.

claim: Although CLE-derived cells were able to enter the notochord domain, they were unable to differentiate correctly.
source: Therefore, although they were able to enter the notochord domain, they were unable to differentiate correctly, suggesting that E8.5 NMPs are not notochord progenitors.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of proper notochord marker expression in grafted cells.

claim: E8.5 NMPs are not notochord progenitors.
source: Therefore, although they were able to enter the notochord domain, they were unable to differentiate correctly, suggesting that E8.5 NMPs are not notochord progenitors.
evidence: Inferred from the inability of CLE-derived cells to properly differentiate as notochord.

claim: The posterior notochord is derived from nodal positive cells in the mesoderm adjacent to the node.
source: This is consistent with fate mapping studies indicating that the posterior notochord is derived from nodal positive cells in the mesoderm adjacent to the node (Brennan et al., 2002) and that convergent extension is the main driver of notochord extension at early somite stages (Yamanaka et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited fate mapping studies.

claim: Convergent extension is the main driver of notochord extension at early somite stages.
source: This is consistent with fate mapping studies indicating that the posterior notochord is derived from nodal positive cells in the mesoderm adjacent to the node (Brennan et al., 2002) and that convergent extension is the main driver of notochord extension at early somite stages (Yamanaka et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited study on notochord morphogenesis.

claim: From E8.5 onwards the notochord may elongate primarily as a result of rearrangement of pre-existing notochord progenitors rather than de novo addition of cells from the epiblast layer.
source: Together, these results suggest that from E8.5 onwards the notochord may elongate primarily as a result of rearrangement of pre-existing notochord progenitors rather than de novo addition of cells from the epiblast layer.
evidence: Inferred from the grafting results and cited studies on notochord development.

claim: Grafting L2-3 progenitors to the midline NSB changed their respective neural versus mesodermal contribution.
source: Grafting L2-3 progenitors to the midline NSB not only changed their respective neural versus mesodermal contribution (shown as the percentage of all sections for a given series; Figure 8A), but also increased their CNH contribution (from 20% to 42% of sections), suggesting that a midline position favours NMP maintenance throughout axis elongation.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative comparison of homotopic and heterotopic grafts shown in Figure 8.

claim: Grafting L2-3 progenitors to the midline NSB increased their CNH contribution from 20% to 42% of sections.
source: Grafting L2-3 progenitors to the midline NSB not only changed their respective neural versus mesodermal contribution (shown as the percentage of all sections for a given series; Figure 8A), but also increased their CNH contribution (from 20% to 42% of sections), suggesting that a midline position favours NMP maintenance throughout axis elongation.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 8.

claim: A midline position favours NMP maintenance throughout axis elongation.
source: Grafting L2-3 progenitors to the midline NSB not only changed their respective neural versus mesodermal contribution (shown as the percentage of all sections for a given series; Figure 8A), but also increased their CNH contribution (from 20% to 42% of sections), suggesting that a midline position favours NMP maintenance throughout axis elongation.
evidence: Inferred from the increased CNH contribution when cells are placed in midline position.

claim: CLE homotopic grafts predominantly contributed to lateral regions of the neural tube in the axis, but shifted towards the midline in the tail bud.
source: CLE homotopic grafts predominantly contributed to lateral regions of the NT in the axis, but shifted towards the midline in the tail bud (Figure 6Aa–h and Aq–t), indicating that there is a net displacement of at least some of the CLE cells towards the midline as axis elongation proceeds, perhaps to replace cells that have exited to the mesoderm via the midline PS.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of dorsoventral NT contribution shown in figures.

claim: There is a net displacement of at least some of the CLE cells towards the midline as axis elongation proceeds.
source: CLE homotopic grafts predominantly contributed to lateral regions of the NT in the axis, but shifted towards the midline in the tail bud (Figure 6Aa–h and Aq–t), indicating that there is a net displacement of at least some of the CLE cells towards the midline as axis elongation proceeds, perhaps to replace cells that have exited to the mesoderm via the midline PS.
evidence: Inferred from the shift in NT contribution pattern from axis to tail bud.

claim: CLE cells grafted to the NSB appeared to have erased their positional bias, as NT contribution was predominantly midline in both axis and tail bud sections.
source: CLE cells grafted to the NSB appeared to have erased their positional bias, as NT contribution was predominantly midline in both axis and TB sections (Figure 8C); a contribution pattern which strongly resembled NSB homotopic grafts previously described in (Cambray and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of dorsoventral NT contribution shown in Figure 8.

claim: The NT contribution pattern of CLE cells grafted to NSB strongly resembled NSB homotopic grafts.
source: CLE cells grafted to the NSB appeared to have erased their positional bias, as NT contribution was predominantly midline in both axis and TB sections (Figure 8C); a contribution pattern which strongly resembled NSB homotopic grafts previously described in (Cambray and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison with previously published data.

claim: Positional information in neural progenitors can be reset, arguing for the existence of a single NMP identity whose fate and dorsoventral NT position is instructed by positional cues.
source: Thus, as positional information in neural progenitors can be reset, it argues for the existence of a single NMP identity whose fate and dorsoventral NT position is instructed by positional cues.
evidence: Inferred from the ability of grafted cells to adopt the positional characteristics of their new environment.

claim: Inhibiting Wnt signalling can divert predominantly mesoderm-fated cells in early zebrafish embryos towards neural fates.
source: Inhibiting Wnt signalling can divert predominantly mesoderm-fated cells in early zebrafish embryos towards neural fates (Martin and Kimelman, 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited study in zebrafish.

claim: In mouse, β-catenin is required for mesoderm differentiation in primitive streak/tail bud cells.
source: Conditional deletion of Wnt3a or β-catenin in the T-expressing population, followed by lineage tracing, has confirmed that, in mouse, β-catenin is required for mesoderm differentiation in PS/TB cells (Garriock et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited lineage-tracing study.

claim: All control L1-3 to St1-3 AGFP7 grafts contributed extensively to the paraxial mesoderm and tail bud mesoderm.
source: As expected, all control L1-3 to St1-3 AGFP7 grafts (n = 4) contributed extensively to the PXM and TBM.
evidence: Demonstrated by control grafting experiments.

claim: With the exception of a few cells in a single embryo, the CNH was not colonised by control L1-3 to St1-3 AGFP7 grafts.
source: With the exception of a few cells in a single embryo, the CNH was not colonised (Figure 9—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by control grafting experiments shown in figure supplement.

claim: 4-OHT-treated βcatCKO:sGFP donor cells that exited the primitive streak early produced exclusively mesoderm.
source: Similarly, the 4-OHT-treated βcatCKO:sGFP donor cells that exited the PS early, and thus contributed to rostral parts of the axis, produced exclusively mesoderm.
evidence: Demonstrated by β-catenin deletion grafting experiments.

claim: 4-OHT-treated βcatCKO:sGFP donor cells exiting later to caudal regions produced only neurectoderm.
source: In contrast, those exiting later to caudal regions produced only neurectoderm (nembryos=11; 9/9 incorporated grafts switched from PXM to neural fate, Figure 9A).
evidence: Demonstrated by β-catenin deletion grafting experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: GFP+ cells in β-catenin-deleted grafts generally showed undetectable levels of β-catenin but expressed N-cadherin at levels similar to neighbouring wildtype cells.
source: GFP+ cells generally showed undetectable levels of β-catenin, but expressed the cell adhesion molecule N-cadherin at levels similar to neighbouring wildtype cells, suggesting that their cell adhesion properties remain intact (Figure 9B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 9.

claim: Graft-derived cells in the paraxial mesoderm correctly expressed Pax3.
source: Graft-derived cells in the PXM correctly expressed Pax3, while those in the NT expressed neural markers (Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 2G), showing that β-catenin deletion does not preclude either neural or mesoderm differentiation after cells have exited from the NMP compartment.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in figures.

claim: Graft-derived cells in the neural tube expressed neural markers.
source: Graft-derived cells in the PXM correctly expressed Pax3, while those in the NT expressed neural markers (Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 2G), showing that β-catenin deletion does not preclude either neural or mesoderm differentiation after cells have exited from the NMP compartment.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in figures.

claim: β-catenin deletion does not preclude either neural or mesoderm differentiation after cells have exited from the NMP compartment.
source: Graft-derived cells in the PXM correctly expressed Pax3, while those in the NT expressed neural markers (Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 2G), showing that β-catenin deletion does not preclude either neural or mesoderm differentiation after cells have exited from the NMP compartment.
evidence: Inferred from the proper expression of lineage markers in β-catenin-deleted cells.

claim: The decision of NMPs to form mesoderm depends absolutely on β-catenin, and in its absence, cells differentiate to neural derivatives.
source: Thus, the decision of NMPs to form mesoderm depends absolutely on β-catenin, and in its absence, cells differentiate to neural derivatives.
evidence: Demonstrated by the complete switch from mesoderm to neural fate in β-catenin-deleted NMP grafts.

claim: Compared to wildtype controls, the notochord extended further caudally in β-catenin-deleted embryos.
source: Compared to wildtype controls, the notochord extended further caudally than in wildtype embryos and the size of the NMP region was reduced in 4-OHT-treated βcatCKO and Sox2+T+ cells appeared scattered throughout the CLE (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis of whole embryos shown in figures.

claim: The size of the NMP region was reduced in 4-OHT-treated βcatCKO embryos.
source: Compared to wildtype controls, the notochord extended further caudally than in wildtype embryos and the size of the NMP region was reduced in 4-OHT-treated βcatCKO and Sox2+T+ cells appeared scattered throughout the CLE (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis shown in figures.

claim: Sox2+T+ cells appeared scattered throughout the CLE in 4-OHT-treated βcatCKO embryos.
source: Compared to wildtype controls, the notochord extended further caudally than in wildtype embryos and the size of the NMP region was reduced in 4-OHT-treated βcatCKO and Sox2+T+ cells appeared scattered throughout the CLE (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis shown in figures.

claim: A significant drop in Sox2+T+ cell numbers was observed in E9.5 β-catenin-deleted samples.
source: We observed a significant drop in Sox2+T+ cell numbers in E9.5 treated samples (Figure 9C and Video 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data shown in figures.

claim: The number of Sox2+T+ cells in E9.5 β-catenin-deleted embryos was not significantly different from untreated E8.5 samples, indicating a failure to expand NMP numbers.
source: Moreover, the number of Sox2+T+ cells in E9.5 β-catenin-deleted embryos was not significantly different from untreated E8.5 samples, indicating a failure to expand NMP numbers (Figure 9D).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 9.

claim: A significant drop in Sox2-T+ cell numbers was observed in β-catenin-deleted embryos.
source: We observed a significant drop in Sox2-T+ cell numbers (Figure 9E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H), consistent with the observation that T is a direct transcriptional target of Wnt signalling via β-catenin (Yamaguchi et al., 1999).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in figures.

claim: T is a direct transcriptional target of Wnt signalling via β-catenin.
source: We observed a significant drop in Sox2-T+ cell numbers (Figure 9E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H), consistent with the observation that T is a direct transcriptional target of Wnt signalling via β-catenin (Yamaguchi et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by cited molecular study.

claim: The number of cells expressing all but the highest levels of T was significantly reduced in 4-OHT-treated βcatCKO embryos.
source: The number of cells expressing all but the highest levels of T was significantly reduced in 4-OHT-treated βcatCKO embryos (Figure 9H and Figure 9—figure supplement 3C), whereas the T- fraction was significantly increased.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative 3D analysis shown in figures.

claim: The T- fraction was significantly increased in 4-OHT-treated βcatCKO embryos.
source: The number of cells expressing all but the highest levels of T was significantly reduced in 4-OHT-treated βcatCKO embryos (Figure 9H and Figure 9—figure supplement 3C), whereas the T- fraction was significantly increased.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative 3D analysis shown in figures.

claim: Wnt signalling is required for NMP expansion, at least in part through the maintenance of T.
source: Thus, Wnt signalling is required for NMP expansion, at least in part through the maintenance of T.
evidence: Inferred from the failure of NMP expansion and T downregulation in β-catenin-deleted embryos.

claim: The maintenance of T in LPMPs and their descendants is less dependent on β-catenin.
source: Moreover, our data suggests the maintenance of T in LPMPs and their descendants is less dependent on β-catenin.
evidence: Inferred from the retention of higher T levels in LPMP-derived tissues compared to NMP-derived tissues in β-catenin-deleted embryos.

claim: LPMPs may represent an alternative, β-catenin-independent route towards mesoderm formation.
source: Therefore, LPMPs may represent an alternative, β-catenin-independent route towards mesoderm formation.
evidence: Inferred from the differential β-catenin dependence of LPMPs versus NMPs.

claim: L/St5 cells grafted to the rostral primitive streak (St1-3) contributed robustly to both paraxial mesoderm and lateral/ventral mesoderm.
source: We grafted L/St5 cells to the rostral PS (St1-3; embryos 7.01–7.03); a region that contributes extensively to paraxial mesoderm (Cambray and Wilson, 2007). In this location, L/St5 cells contributed robustly to both PXM and LVM.
evidence: Demonstrated by heterotopic grafting experiments.

claim: Similar to homotopic St1 grafts, L/St5 to St1-3 grafts contributed to the tail bud mesoderm but not chordoneural hinge.
source: Similar to homotopic St1 grafts, L/St5 to St1-3 grafts contributed to the TBM but not CNH (Figure 10Aa–e and Cambray and Wilson (2007)).
evidence: Demonstrated by heterotopic grafting experiments and comparison with previous data.

claim: Contribution to the tail bud mesoderm was limited in L/St5 to St1-3 grafts.
source: However contribution to the TBM was limited (Figure 10Ae,B,D and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in figures.

claim: Caudal-most CLE progenitors show plasticity within the mesoderm lineage.
source: Hence, these caudal-most CLE progenitors show plasticity within the mesoderm lineage.
evidence: Inferred from the ability of L/St5 cells to form both PXM and LVM when grafted to rostral PS.

claim: β-catenin deleted L/St5 cells formed only paraxial mesoderm and lateral/ventral mesoderm without neural tube differentiation.
source: Unlike rostral CLE, β-catenin deleted L/St5 cells formed only PXM and LVM without NT differentiation (Figure 10Af–j).
evidence: Demonstrated by β-catenin deletion grafting experiments shown in Figure 10.

claim: β-catenin is not required for L/St5 cells to undergo mesoderm differentiation.
source: Thus, β-catenin is not required for L/St5 cells to undergo mesoderm differentiation.
evidence: Demonstrated by the continued mesoderm formation in β-catenin-deleted L/St5 grafts.

claim: All L/St5 to Br grafts showed exclusively mesodermal contribution except for a small patch in the neural tube of one embryo.
source: All L/St5 to Br grafts showed exclusively mesodermal contribution except for a small patch in the NT of one embryo (embryo 8.03; Figure 10Ak–o,C–E and Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by heterotopic grafting experiments shown in figures.

claim: Environmental cues can switch the exclusive LVM fate of at least some L/St5 cells to include paraxial mesoderm.
source: Thus, environmental cues can switch the exclusive LVM fate of at least some L/St5 cells to include PXM, but they do not adopt neural fates, even where L1-3 cells undergo predominantly neural differentiation.
evidence: Demonstrated by heterotopic grafting experiments showing PXM contribution but no neural contribution.

claim: L/St5 cells do not adopt neural fates, even where L1-3 cells undergo predominantly neural differentiation.
source: Thus, environmental cues can switch the exclusive LVM fate of at least some L/St5 cells to include PXM, but they do not adopt neural fates, even where L1-3 cells undergo predominantly neural differentiation.
evidence: Demonstrated by heterotopic grafting experiments showing absence of neural contribution.

claim: Sox2 is absent in the caudal-most tip of the CLE.
source: We have shown above that Sox2 is absent in the caudal-most tip of the CLE (Figure 3Bf and 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis shown in figures.

claim: Sox2, together with Sox3, is required for neural differentiation.
source: This transcription factor, together with Sox3, is required for neural differentiation, and can reinstate neural differentiation when ectopically expressed in emergent PXM (Takemoto et al., 2011; Yoshida et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited molecular studies.

claim: Sox2 can reinstate neural differentiation when ectopically expressed in emergent paraxial mesoderm.
source: This transcription factor, together with Sox3, is required for neural differentiation, and can reinstate neural differentiation when ectopically expressed in emergent PXM (Takemoto et al., 2011; Yoshida et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited molecular studies.

claim: Cells that did not take up the Sox2 expression vector incorporated well and contributed to the paraxial mesoderm.
source: Cells that did not take up the vector incorporated well and contributed to the PXM as before.
evidence: Demonstrated by electroporation and grafting experiments.

claim: tdTomato-expressing cells (Sox2-overexpressing) formed non-integrated clumps along the axis.
source: In contrast, tdTomato-expressing cells formed non-integrated clumps along the axis (Figure 10F).
evidence: Demonstrated by electroporation and grafting experiments shown in Figure 10.

claim: No evidence of neural differentiation was apparent in electroporated cells overexpressing Sox2.
source: No evidence of neural differentiation was apparent in electroporated cells (nembryos = 6).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of Sox2-overexpressing grafted cells.

claim: Ectopic expression of Sox2 is unable to override the inability of L/St5 cells to contribute to the neural tube.
source: Thus, ectopic expression of Sox2 is unable to override the inability of L/St5 cells to contribute to the NT.
evidence: Demonstrated by Sox2 overexpression experiments showing no neural differentiation.

claim: Fate and potency mapping, together with genetic manipulation, have allowed definition of two populations of progenitors, NMPs and LPMPs, residing in the primitive streak region.
source: Fate and potency mapping, together with genetic manipulation, have allowed us to define two populations of progenitors, NMPs and LPMPs, residing in the primitive streak region.
evidence: Summary of the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Distinct regulatory logics govern the intrinsic abilities of NMPs and LPMPs to respond to their environment.
source: Distinct regulatory logics govern their intrinsic abilities to respond to their environment (Figure 11).
evidence: Inferred from the differential responses to β-catenin deletion and Sox2 overexpression.

claim: These lineage-restricted progenitors in E8.5 embryos emerge from the pluripotent epiblast at the beginning of somitogenesis.
source: These lineage-restricted progenitors in E8.5 embryos emerge from the pluripotent epiblast at the beginning of somitogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the timing of lineage restriction shown by kidney capsule grafts.

claim: The lineage restriction of these populations, together with their lack of neoplastic potential, may render them useful for clinical applications.
source: The lineage restriction of these populations, together with their lack of neoplastic potential, may render them useful for clinical applications.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the characterized properties of the progenitor populations.

claim: The Sox2+T+ phenotype overlaps extensively with NM potency.
source: Despite previous reports that Sox2+T+ positivity identifies NMPs, no study has previously comprehensively correlated this phenotype with the known spatiotemporal characteristics of NMPs. Our immunohistochemical analysis shows that Sox2+T+cells are found in all NMP-containing regions: the NSB, rostral CLE, and the ectoderm of the CNH during throughout axis elongation, and are undetectable once somitogenesis ceases, suggesting they are associated with NMP activity.
evidence: Demonstrated by comprehensive spatiotemporal correlation analysis.

claim: The increase in Sox2+T+ cell numbers between E8.5 and E9.5 is similar to the increase in NMP numbers estimated from clonal analysis.
source: Secondly, clonal analysis indicates that the number of NMPs present at E9.5 is approximately 2.8-fold greater than that at E8.5 (5 NM clones with a rostral limit of s10-20, versus 14 with a rostral limit of s21-30 (Tzouanacou et al., 2009)). This increase is similar to the 2.4-fold increase in number of Sox2+T+ cells during this period (960 ± 85 versus 2338 ± 176; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of quantitative data with published clonal analysis.

claim: Single positive T+ and Sox2+ cells can be derived from Sox2+T+ cells in vitro.
source: Furthermore, in vitro data shows that single positive T+ and Sox2+ cells can be derived from Sox2+T+ cells (Tsakiridis and Wilson, 2015), and cell clusters comprising 60–80% Sox2+T+ cells derived from pluripotent populations in vitro contribute to neural and mesoderm lineages when engrafted in the E8.5 embryo (Gouti et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited in vitro studies.

claim: Cell clusters comprising 60–80% Sox2+T+ cells derived from pluripotent populations in vitro contribute to neural and mesoderm lineages when engrafted in the E8.5 embryo.
source: Furthermore, in vitro data shows that single positive T+ and Sox2+ cells can be derived from Sox2+T+ cells (Tsakiridis and Wilson, 2015), and cell clusters comprising 60–80% Sox2+T+ cells derived from pluripotent populations in vitro contribute to neural and mesoderm lineages when engrafted in the E8.5 embryo (Gouti et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited in vitro and grafting study.

claim: The marker combination Sox2+T+ is useful for prospectively identifying NMPs both in vivo and in vitro.
source: Taken together, this indicates that this marker combination is useful for prospectively identifying NMPs both in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive correlation between Sox2+T+ phenotype and NMP characteristics.

claim: Within the Sox2+T+ population, clear differences in levels of Sox2 and T appear to reflect greater likelihood to adopt neural and mesodermal fates respectively.
source: Interestingly, within the Sox2+T+ population, we show clear differences in levels of Sox2 and T (Figure 5A) and these appear to reflect greater likelihood to adopt neural and mesodermal fates respectively.
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation between expression levels and fate outcomes.

claim: The levels of Sox2 and T may report on the cells' responses to environmental cues directing their fate.
source: Together with the observation that all L1-3 regions show equivalent potential on grafting to the NSB, this suggests that the levels of each protein may report on the cells' responses to environmental cues directing their fate.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between expression levels and position-dependent fate outcomes.

claim: The differences in NSB and CLE fate do not result from intrinsic differences between the populations, but rather from the different environmental influences that they are exposed to in vivo.
source: However the data presented here argue for a single, adaptable NMP type, since rostral CLE cells show equal potential to contribute to the CNH, as well as both neural and mesodermal fates over long axial distances, in the context of the NSB environment. Thus the differences in NSB and CLE fate do not result from intrinsic differences between the populations, but rather from the different environmental influences that they are exposed to in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the equivalent potential shown by CLE cells when grafted to NSB.

claim: Single-cell labelling experiments in HH4-9 chick embryos show that very few cells in the node region are fated solely for neural tube.
source: This is consistent with single-cell labelling experiments HH4-9 chick embryos, which show that very few cells in the node region are fated solely for neural tube (Selleck and Stern, 1991).
evidence: Supported by cited single-cell labelling study in chick.

claim: Clonal analysis in the mouse shows that medium-length mesoderm-only clones outnumber neuromesodermal clones (50 in mesoderm vs 8 NM).
source: Clonal analysis in the mouse shows that medium-length mesoderm-only clones outnumber neuromesodermal clones (50 in mesoderm vs 8 NM; (Tzouanacou et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by cited clonal analysis study.

claim: The overproduction of mesoderm relative to neurectoderm may begin to be implemented in the primitive streak/tail bud region in the NMPs themselves.
source: Since the volume of differentiated paraxial mesoderm is always greater than that of the neurectoderm, the overproduction of mesoderm relative to neurectoderm may begin to be implemented in the primitive streak/tail bud region in the NMPs themselves.
evidence: Inferred from the fate mapping data showing more mesoderm than neural contribution.

claim: Regulation of NMP proliferation/survival and differentiation may begin the process of determining the final proportions of neurectoderm and mesoderm in the embryonic axis.
source: Together with the correlation between the mid-trunk expansion of NMPs and the size of the somites (Tam, 1981), this implies that regulation of NMP proliferation/survival and differentiation may begin the process of determining the final proportions of neurectoderm and mesoderm in the embryonic axis.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between NMP numbers and tissue proportions.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin control of neural versus mesodermal fate choice is a vertebrate-wide phenomenon.
source: In zebrafish, downregulation of Wnt/β-catenin activity diverts cells fated for mesoderm towards neurectoderm, demonstrating that Wnt/β-catenin control of neural versus mesodermal fate choice is a vertebrate-wide phenomenon (Martin and Kimelman, 2012).
evidence: Supported by comparison with zebrafish data.

claim: The transcriptional downregulation of many Wnt pathway components in the emerging committed neurectoderm relative to the CLE is consistent with a role for Wnt downregulation in neural differentiation from NMPs.
source: The transcriptional downregulation of many Wnt pathway components in the emerging committed neurectoderm relative to the CLE is consistent with a role for Wnt downregulation in neural differentiation from NMPs (Olivera-Martinez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited transcriptional profiling study.

claim: A decline in Wnt3a expression in the elongating tail occurs in tandem with the gradual loss of Sox2+T+ cells.
source: A decline in Wnt3a expression in the elongating tail (Cambray and Wilson, 2007) occurs in tandem with the gradual loss of Sox2+T+ cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation between Wnt3a expression and Sox2+T+ cell numbers.

claim: It is likely that Wnt signalling is required for NMP maintenance.
source: Therefore it is likely that Wnt signalling is required for NMP maintenance.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between Wnt3a expression and NMP numbers, and the failure of NMP expansion in β-catenin-deleted embryos.

claim: The short axis of mutants with lowered Wnt3a levels is due to a failure to maintain NMPs.
source: This suggests that the short axis of mutants with lowered Wnt3a levels (Greco et al., 1996; Takada et al., 1994) is due to a failure to maintain NMPs.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of Wnt signalling for NMP maintenance.

claim: T is dramatically downregulated in the caudal epiblast when β-catenin is depleted.
source: Since, we show that T is dramatically downregulated in the caudal epiblast when β-catenin is depleted, (Figure 9G), this raises the possibility that T is necessary for NMP maintenance.
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: T may be necessary for NMP maintenance.
source: Since, we show that T is dramatically downregulated in the caudal epiblast when β-catenin is depleted, (Figure 9G), this raises the possibility that T is necessary for NMP maintenance.
evidence: Speculative inference from the correlation between T levels and NMP maintenance.

claim: Posterior Hox gene activation in chick leads to downregulation of Wnt signalling, and of T expression, slowing of cell ingression from the ectoderm layer and shortening of the presomitic mesoderm.
source: Interestingly, a recent study (Denans et al., 2015) shows that posterior Hox gene activation in chick leads to downregulation of Wnt signalling, and of T expression, slowing of cell ingression from the ectoderm layer and shortening of the PSM.
evidence: Supported by cited study in chick.

claim: The equivalent late axial elongation period in mouse begins around the trunk/tail transition, when the number of NMPs begins to decline.
source: The equivalent late axial elongation period in mouse begins around the trunk/tail transition (Gomez et al., 2008), when the number of NMPs begins to decline.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of NMP numbers and cited study on axial elongation.

claim: The effects of posterior Hox genes on axial elongation operate in NMPs themselves via Wnt/β-catenin-mediated control of progenitor numbers.
source: Our data argues that the effects of posterior Hox genes on axial elongation operate in NMPs themselves via Wnt/β-catenin-mediated control of progenitor numbers (Figure 11B).
evidence: Inferred from the role of Wnt/β-catenin in NMP expansion and the effects of Hox genes on Wnt signalling.

claim: Providing the T+ caudal region with a stabilised form of β-catenin, or overexpressing Wnt3a in T+ or Cdx2+ progenitors, results in an enlarged presomitic mesoderm domain but not an obvious reduction in Sox2+T+ NMPs in the CLE.
source: Providing the T+ caudal region with a stabilised form of β-catenin, or overexpressing Wnt3a in T+ or Cdx2+ progenitors, results in an enlarged PSM domain (Garriock et al., 2015; Aulehla et al., 2008; Jurberg et al., 2014) but not an obvious reduction in Sox2+T+ NMPs in the CLE (Garriock et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited genetic manipulation studies.

claim: When β-catenin is deleted, Sox2+T+ NMPs are significantly reduced in number, but are not completely eliminated from the caudal region.
source: Here we show that, when β-catenin is deleted, Sox2+T+ NMPs are significantly reduced in number, but are not completely eliminated from the caudal region.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of Sox2+T+ cells in β-catenin-deleted embryos.

claim: Elevated Wnt/β-catenin signalling alone is not enough to commit NMPs to a mesoderm fate, but its absence is sufficient to block mesoderm differentiation.
source: Taken together, these results show that elevated Wnt/β-catenin signalling alone is not enough to commit NMPs to a mesoderm fate, but its absence is sufficient to block mesoderm differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of gain-of-function and loss-of-function experiments.

claim: Additional signalling pathway(s) are implicated in driving NMPs towards mesoderm formation.
source: This implicates additional signalling pathway(s) in driving NMPs towards mesoderm formation.
evidence: Inferred from the insufficiency of Wnt/β-catenin alone to commit NMPs to mesoderm.

claim: Despite the requirement for Wnt signalling in expanding NMP numbers, at least some NMPs can tolerate both elevated and reduced levels of Wnt signalling for short (24–48 hr) periods.
source: Moreover, despite the requirement for Wnt signalling in expanding NMP numbers, at least some NMPs can tolerate both elevated and reduced levels of Wnt signalling, at least for short (24–48 hr) periods.
evidence: Inferred from the persistence of some Sox2+T+ cells under altered Wnt signalling conditions.

claim: Nuclear β-catenin staining in the zebrafish tail bud has shown that canonical Wnt signalling is only moderately active in NMPs and high in early differentiating mesodermal cells.
source: Nuclear β-catenin staining in the zebrafish tail bud has shown that canonical Wnt signalling is only moderately active in NMPs and high in early differentiating mesodermal cells (Bouldin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited study in zebrafish.

claim: Wnt3a is expressed uniformly in the E8.5 caudal region.
source: Since Wnt3a is expressed uniformly in the E8.5 caudal region (Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Takada et al., 1994), it is unlikely that localisation of Wnt3a itself can provide the specificity to direct mesoderm formation from NMPs.
evidence: Supported by cited expression studies.

claim: It is unlikely that localisation of Wnt3a itself can provide the specificity to direct mesoderm formation from NMPs.
source: Since Wnt3a is expressed uniformly in the E8.5 caudal region (Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Takada et al., 1994), it is unlikely that localisation of Wnt3a itself can provide the specificity to direct mesoderm formation from NMPs.
evidence: Inferred from the uniform expression pattern of Wnt3a.

claim: Wnt modulators might provide the signal specificity to direct mesoderm formation from NMPs.
source: It is therefore possible that Wnt modulators might provide this signal.
evidence: Speculative inference from the need for signal specificity.

claim: R-spondin3 is transcribed in the presomitic mesoderm.
