source: R-spondin3, an extracellular Wnt activator, is transcribed in the PSM (Kazanskaya et al., 2004) and has recently been shown to drive pluripotent cells towards skeletal muscle derivatives in vitro (Chal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited expression study.

claim: R-spondin3 has been shown to drive pluripotent cells towards skeletal muscle derivatives in vitro.
source: R-spondin3, an extracellular Wnt activator, is transcribed in the PSM (Kazanskaya et al., 2004) and has recently been shown to drive pluripotent cells towards skeletal muscle derivatives in vitro (Chal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited in vitro study.

claim: Fgf signalling, steroid biogenesis and chondroitin sulphate biosynthesis were identified as differentially regulated between NMPs and committed neural progenitors in chick.
source: Fgf signalling, as well as steroid biogenesis and chondroitin sulphate biosynthesis were identified as differentially regulated between NMPs and committed neural progenitors in chick (Olivera-Martinez et al., 2014), and it remains to be seen whether these play a role in coordinating the balance between neural and mesoderm differentiation in all vertebrates.
evidence: Supported by cited transcriptional profiling study in chick.

claim: Mouse embryos lacking Wnt3a or β-catenin in the primitive streak are still able to form rostral paraxial mesoderm.
source: However, mouse embryos lacking Wnt3a or β-catenin in the primitive streak are still able to form rostral paraxial mesoderm, (Aulehla et al., 2008; Takada et al., 1994), suggesting the mesoderm-inducing signals acting on the early progenitors of paraxial mesoderm must be different from those at later times.
evidence: Supported by cited genetic studies.

claim: The mesoderm-inducing signals acting on the early progenitors of paraxial mesoderm must be different from those at later times.
source: However, mouse embryos lacking Wnt3a or β-catenin in the primitive streak are still able to form rostral paraxial mesoderm, (Aulehla et al., 2008; Takada et al., 1994), suggesting the mesoderm-inducing signals acting on the early progenitors of paraxial mesoderm must be different from those at later times.
evidence: Inferred from the ability to form mesoderm without Wnt3a/β-catenin at early stages.

claim: LPMPs are less dependent on Wnt/β-catenin signalling for T maintenance.
source: Moreover, our data suggests that LPMPs are less dependent on Wnt/β-catenin signalling for T maintenance, and that additional signalling could be an important regulator of this population.
evidence: Demonstrated by retention of T expression in LPMP-derived tissues in β-catenin-deleted embryos.

claim: Additional signalling could be an important regulator of the LPMP population.
source: Moreover, our data suggests that LPMPs are less dependent on Wnt/β-catenin signalling for T maintenance, and that additional signalling could be an important regulator of this population.
evidence: Speculative inference from the differential Wnt/β-catenin dependence.

claim: Bmp4 and Bmp7 are expressed in the caudal CLE.
source: Bmp4 and Bmp7 are expressed in the caudal CLE (Arkell and Beddington, 1997; Fujiwara et al., 2002) and have been implicated in the upregulation of T during mesoderm differentiation from embryonic stem cells (Suzuki et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by cited expression studies.

claim: Bmp4 and Bmp7 have been implicated in the upregulation of T during mesoderm differentiation from embryonic stem cells.
source: Bmp4 and Bmp7 are expressed in the caudal CLE (Arkell and Beddington, 1997; Fujiwara et al., 2002) and have been implicated in the upregulation of T during mesoderm differentiation from embryonic stem cells (Suzuki et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by cited in vitro study.

claim: LPMPs are regulated differently from NMPs.
source: Together with the inability of forced Sox2 expression to direct integration in the NT, our results indicate that LPMPs are regulated differently from NMPs.
evidence: Inferred from the differential responses to β-catenin deletion and Sox2 overexpression.

claim: LPMPs can participate in paraxial mesoderm production.
source: We also show that LPMPs can participate in PXM production, consistent with clonal data showing that mesoderm-restricted clones can contribute to both PXM and LVM (Tzouanacou et al., 2009).
evidence: Demonstrated by heterotopic grafting experiments and supported by cited clonal analysis.

claim: L/St5 cells normally never contribute to the paraxial mesoderm.
source: Our fate map shows that L/St5 cells normally never contribute to the PXM, suggesting that LPMPs choose lateral mesoderm fates over paraxial ones based on their position.
evidence: Demonstrated by homotopic grafting experiments.

claim: LPMPs choose lateral mesoderm fates over paraxial ones based on their position.
source: Our fate map shows that L/St5 cells normally never contribute to the PXM, suggesting that LPMPs choose lateral mesoderm fates over paraxial ones based on their position.
evidence: Inferred from the position-dependent fate outcomes in grafting experiments.

claim: NMP numbers peak through the actions of Wnt/β-catenin signalling during trunk-to-tail transition.
source: Here we show NMP numbers peak through the actions of Wnt/β-catenin signalling during trunk-to-tail transition.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of NMP numbers and β-catenin deletion experiments.

claim: The role of β-catenin in NMP maintenance/expansion may be cell-autonomous.
source: This role of β-catenin in NMP maintenance/expansion may be cell-autonomous, although it is also possible that it acts in neighbouring notochord progenitors.
evidence: Speculative inference from the experimental results.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signalling is high in the notochord region throughout axis elongation and is required in the notochord itself for notochord integrity and tail growth.
source: Wnt/β-catenin signalling is high in this region throughout axis elongation and is required in the notochord itself for notochord integrity and tail growth (Ukita et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by cited study on notochord development.

claim: Abnormalities in the caudal notochord are present in embryos depleted for β-catenin between E8.5–9.5.
source: Abnormalities in the caudal notochord are also present in embryos depleted for β-catenin between E8.5–9.5 (Figure 9Cd–f), and the distance between the NMP area and the caudal notochord apparently increased (Figure 9G).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of β-catenin-deleted embryos shown in Figure 9.

claim: The distance between the NMP area and the caudal notochord apparently increased in β-catenin-depleted embryos.
source: Abnormalities in the caudal notochord are also present in embryos depleted for β-catenin between E8.5–9.5 (Figure 9Cd–f), and the distance between the NMP area and the caudal notochord apparently increased (Figure 9G).
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: The level of T in the notochord is far less affected compared to other tail bud domains in β-catenin-deleted embryos.
source: Despite the structural aberrations in βcatCKO embryos, the level of T in the notochord is far less affected compared to other tail bud domains (Figure 9Gd), suggesting T expression is uncoupled from Wnt/β-catenin signalling in these cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D analysis of T levels shown in Figure 9.

claim: T expression is uncoupled from Wnt/β-catenin signalling in notochord cells.
source: Despite the structural aberrations in βcatCKO embryos, the level of T in the notochord is far less affected compared to other tail bud domains (Figure 9Gd), suggesting T expression is uncoupled from Wnt/β-catenin signalling in these cells.
evidence: Inferred from the retention of T expression in notochord despite β-catenin deletion.

claim: Notochordal cells are found close to NMPs in the NSB but not in the CLE.
source: Notochordal cells are found close to NMPs in the NSB but not in the CLE, arguing against the idea that the presence of the notochord environment is absolutely essential for NMP identity.
evidence: Based on anatomical observations.

claim: The presence of the notochord environment is not absolutely essential for NMP identity.
source: Notochordal cells are found close to NMPs in the NSB but not in the CLE, arguing against the idea that the presence of the notochord environment is absolutely essential for NMP identity.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of NMPs in CLE without adjacent notochord.

claim: The NMP pool is only maintained over long axial distances adjacent to the caudal notochord tip.
source: However, since the NMP pool is only maintained over long axial distances adjacent to the caudal notochord tip (Figure 3C-F and Cambray and Wilson (2002); McGrew et al. (2008)), NMP maintenance may be indirectly dependent upon the notochord.
evidence: Demonstrated by spatiotemporal analysis and cited studies.

claim: NMP maintenance may be indirectly dependent upon the notochord.
source: However, since the NMP pool is only maintained over long axial distances adjacent to the caudal notochord tip (Figure 3C-F and Cambray and Wilson (2002); McGrew et al. (2008)), NMP maintenance may be indirectly dependent upon the notochord.
evidence: Inferred from the spatial correlation between NMP maintenance and notochord proximity.

claim: The notochordal 'niche' could include extracellular matrix molecules and secreted factors including Wnts.
source: This notochordal 'niche' could include extracellular matrix molecules, and secreted factors including Wnts.
evidence: Speculative inference about the nature of the notochordal niche.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signalling may act indirectly to maintain the NMP environment.
source: Therefore, Wnt/β-catenin signalling may act indirectly to maintain the NMP environment.
evidence: Speculative inference from the role of Wnt signalling in notochord and NMP maintenance.

claim: LPMPs are likely to interact with NMPs during the time of trunk-to-tail transition.
source: Similarly LPMPs are likely to interact with NMPs during the time of trunk-to-tail transition.
evidence: Inferred from the spatial and temporal proximity of the two populations.

claim: Gdf11 binds Tgfbr1 and activates Isl1 expression in the emerging lateral/ventral mesoderm during trunk-to-tail transition.
source: Gdf11 binds Tgfbr1 and activates Isl1 expression in the emerging LVM during trunk-to-tail transition and provides signals that induce hindlimb bud and cloaca formation (Jurberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited study on Gdf11 function.

claim: Gdf11 provides signals that induce hindlimb bud and cloaca formation.
source: Gdf11 binds Tgfbr1 and activates Isl1 expression in the emerging LVM during trunk-to-tail transition and provides signals that induce hindlimb bud and cloaca formation (Jurberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited study.

claim: Ectopic Isl1 activation in the whole tail bud, including NMPs, leads to complete loss of NM-derived trunk vertebrae and spinal cord.
source: Ectopic Isl1 activation in the whole tail bud, including NMPs, leads to complete loss of NM-derived trunk vertebrae and spinal cord (Jurberg et al., 2013), while loss of Gdf11 function increases the interlimb area by 5 to 6 somites (Jurberg et al., 2013; McPherron et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by cited genetic manipulation studies.

claim: Loss of Gdf11 function increases the interlimb area by 5 to 6 somites.
source: Ectopic Isl1 activation in the whole tail bud, including NMPs, leads to complete loss of NM-derived trunk vertebrae and spinal cord (Jurberg et al., 2013), while loss of Gdf11 function increases the interlimb area by 5 to 6 somites (Jurberg et al., 2013; McPherron et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by cited genetic studies.

claim: Gdf11 acts via LPMPs to attenuate signals that expand the NMP population.
source: This suggests that Gdf11 acts via LPMPs to attenuate signals that expand the NMP population and, together with posterior Hox gene reduction of Wnt signalling (Denans et al., 2015; Young et al., 2009), control the timing of progenitor number reduction in the tail.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of Gdf11 on NMP-derived tissues and its expression in LPMPs.

claim: Gdf11, together with posterior Hox gene reduction of Wnt signalling, controls the timing of progenitor number reduction in the tail.
source: This suggests that Gdf11 acts via LPMPs to attenuate signals that expand the NMP population and, together with posterior Hox gene reduction of Wnt signalling (Denans et al., 2015; Young et al., 2009), control the timing of progenitor number reduction in the tail.
evidence: Inferred from the combined effects of Gdf11 and Hox genes on progenitor populations.

claim: Two separate progenitor types exist in the primitive streak, characterised by differential plasticity and commitment, as well as by the mechanisms by which they choose between alternative fates.
source: In conclusion, we have shown two separate progenitor types exist in the primitive streak, characterised by differential plasticity and commitment, as well as by the mechanisms by which they choose between alternative fates.
evidence: Summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Both NMPs and LPMPs exhibit potency beyond their normal fates, yet this potential is intrinsically constrained in each case.
source: Interestingly, both NMPs and LPMPs exhibit potency beyond their normal fates, yet this potential is intrinsically constrained in each case.
evidence: Demonstrated by heterotopic grafting experiments showing both plasticity and limitations.

claim: These progenitor types can form a paradigm for testing how the interplay between intrinsic competence and extrinsic signals is set up and maintained during cell differentiation.
source: Thus, besides serving as a benchmark for generation of differentiated cell types in vitro, these progenitor types can form a paradigm for testing how the interplay between intrinsic competence and extrinsic signals is set up and maintained during cell differentiation.
evidence: Speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.
